extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, proofreaders, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and evaluating English prose according to the Chicago Manual of Style: punctuation, spelling, syntax, word division, hyphenation, italics/capitals/quotation marks, and related typographic and usage issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing areas for applicants — Punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants will be tested on punctuation: using commas appropriately; deleting unnecessary quotation marks; distinguishing colons from semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing areas for applicants — Spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants will be tested on spelling: using a dictionary appropriately; recognizing homonyms; hyphenating correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing areas for applicants — Syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants will be tested on syntax: matching verb to subject; recognizing and eliminating misplaced modifiers; distinguishing phrases from clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: List hierarchy formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish multiple outline levels by punctuation and indentation so readers see at a glance each item's level; use periods for top three levels and single/double parentheses for lower levels; align multi-digit numerals on the last digit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each division/subdivision should normally contain at least two items; in shorter lists you may dispense with capital roman numerals and capital letters and begin with arabic numerals; examples provided for seven-level outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended dictionaries and single-source consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: For spelling Chicago recommends Merriam‑Webster (Webster’s Third New International and Merriam‑Webster’s Collegiate); when more than one spelling/plural is given, Chicago normally opts for the first form listed; use one source consistently throughout a single work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Collegiate and Third International disagree, follow Collegiate as it represents newer lexical research; consult other standard dictionaries (e.g., American Heritage) for definitions or alternatives; see bibliog. for other English varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific spellings
rubrics_metrics.description: If a variant spelling carries a special connotation within a discipline, respect the author's preference; absent such a preference, prefer the first-listed form in Webster’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'archeology' vs 'archaeology'—if specialists insist on one form respect that choice; Webster’s indicates variants and secondary variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑US spelling in US publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In English-language works by non‑US authors edited/produced in the United States, editors generally change spellings to American forms for consistency; quoted material retains original spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: colour → color; analyse → analyze; authors rarely object to this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementing the dictionary — matters beyond headwords
rubrics_metrics.description: Many matters (plurals, possessives, hyphenation, word breaks, distinctive treatments) are not easily found in dictionaries and are addressed in this chapter; consult Webster’s for base forms but use Chicago guidance for these topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter focuses on forming plurals/possessives of compounds, hyphenation with prefixes/suffixes, line breaks, italics/capitals/quotation marks, etc.; see 7.89 for hyphenation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard plural formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most nouns form plurals by adding -s, or -es after endings ch, j, s, sh, x, or z; dictionaries list irregular plurals and forms that change to -ies or other patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Webster’s Third lists all inflected forms; online dictionaries’ search engines generally return correct plural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative plural forms and usage distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When Webster’s gives two plural forms, Chicago normally opts for the first listed; in some contexts different plural forms serve different purposes (e.g., indexes vs mathematical expressions: 'indexes' vs 'indices').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the first-listed unless a field‑specific usage dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurals of compound nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: For tricky compound plurals consult Webster’s; for those not listed, use common sense to form plurals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fathers‑in‑law, coups d'état, courts‑martial, chefs‑d’œuvre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurals for centuries and ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plural for multiple centuries when joined by 'and' or when expressed with 'through'; use singular for ranges expressed with 'to' or for alternatives with 'or'/'nor'; in compound modifiers use singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries'; 'in the fifth through eighth centuries'; but 'from the twentieth to the twenty‑first century'; compound modifier: 'eighteenth‑ and nineteenth‑century technologies'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurals of proper nouns and family names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of persons and other capitalized nouns normally form the plural by adding s or es; do not use an apostrophe to form the plural of a family name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Toms, Dicks, and Harrys'; 'the Joneses'; 'the Martinez family → the Martinezes'; 'the Jeffersons' not 'Jefferson’s'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural form for Native American group names
rubrics_metrics.description: Defer to the first‑listed form in Webster's for plurals of Native American group names; if not found consult an up‑to‑date encyclopedia or other trusted resource; opt for consistency across names if no preference is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Hopi', 'the Iroquoian language spoken by the Cherokee'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular form used for names ending in unpronounced s or x
rubrics_metrics.description: Names ending in an unpronounced s or x are best left in the singular form when pluralized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the seventeen Louis of France'; 'the two Dumas' (or better, 'two towns called Charlevoix').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural endings for italicized words in roman text
rubrics_metrics.description: If an italicized term requires a plural ending, the s is normally set in roman; titles already in plural form may be left unchanged; if awkward, rephrase to avoid the plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'two Chicago Tribunes and three Milwaukee Journal Sentinels'; 'several Madame Bovarys (or better, several copies of Madame Bovary)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural endings to italicized words in foreign language text
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural endings to italicized words in another language should also be set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Blume, Blumen; cheval, chevaux'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of words in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the plural of a word or phrase in quotation marks in the usual way (without an apostrophe); if the result is awkward, reword to avoid the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'How many more “To be continueds” (not “To be continued”s)?' Better: 'How many more times can we expect to see “To be continued”?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurals of noun coinages and hyphenated phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and hyphenated phrases coined as nouns usually form the plural by adding s or es.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ifs and buts; thank‑yous; dos and don’ts; maybes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurals for letters, abbreviations, and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital letters used as words, numerals used as nouns, and abbreviations usually form the plural by adding s; lowercase letters form the plural with an apostrophe + s to aid comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the three Rs; URLs; x’s and y’s; BSs, MAs, PhDs; the 1990s'.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule for possessives
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive of most singular nouns is formed by adding an apostrophe and s; the possessive of plural nouns ending in s is formed by adding an apostrophe only; see exceptions in 7.20–22.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the horse’s mouth; puppies’ paws; children’s literature'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive of proper nouns, abbreviations, and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The general possessive rule extends to proper nouns (including those ending in s, x, or z), abbreviations, and numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Kansas’s legislature; Tacitus’s Histories; FDR’s legacy; Apollo 11’s fiftieth anniversary'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid possessive for abbreviations followed by spelled-out form
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid forming the possessive of an abbreviation that is immediately followed by a spelled‑out form in parentheses (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the long history of IBM (International Business Machines)' not 'IBM’s (International Business Machines’) long history'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessives of words and names ending in unpronounced s
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and names ending in an unpronounced s form the possessive by adding an apostrophe and s (usually pronounced when spoken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Descartes’s three dreams; the marquis’s mother; Francois’s efforts'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive of classical names ending in eez sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical proper names of two or more syllables that end in an eez sound form the possessive in the usual way, though the additional s is often not pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Euripides’s tragedies; Xerxes’s armies'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions — nouns plural in form but singular in meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When the singular form of a noun ending in s is the same as the plural (uninflected), form the possessive by adding an apostrophe only; if ambiguity results, prefer 'of' phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'politics’ true meaning; economics’ forerunners; this species’ first record (or better, the first record of this species)'; applies also to place/organization names where the last element is plural such as United States’.

rubrics_metrics.name: For... sake expressions and possessive form
rubrics_metrics.description: For a few traditional 'for... sake' expressions with a singular noun ending in s, the possessive may be given by an apostrophe alone for euphony (for goodness’ sake), but the normal possessive form is also acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'for goodness’ sake; for expedience’s sake; for Jesus’s sake'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative practice omitting possessive s on words ending in s (not recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers/publishers prefer omitting the possessive s on words ending in s (e.g., Dylan Thomas’ poetry), but Chicago does not recommend this practice because it disregards pronunciation in most cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint versus separate possession
rubrics_metrics.description: When closely linked nouns possess the same thing, consider them a unit and add the possessive to only the second noun; when possessions are discrete, both nouns take the possessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'my aunt and uncle’s house' (joint); 'my aunt’s and uncle’s medical profiles' (separate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound possessives
rubrics_metrics.description: In compound nouns and noun phrases the final element usually takes the possessive form, even in the plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'student assistants’ time cards; my daughter‑in‑law’s address; my sons‑in‑law’s addresses'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive to mean 'of'
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessive forms may be used analogously to 'of' (in constructions like 'in three days’ time'); if ambiguous or awkward, reword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'in three days’ time (or in three days); an hour’s delay (or a one‑hour delay)'; rephrase if unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double possessive (double genitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A double possessive (a friend of Dick’s) may be used where one of several is implied; do not use a possessive where the meaning is literally 'of' without such implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a friend of Dick’s (or a friend of his)' but not 'a student of Kierkegaard'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive versus attributive forms for groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Although group ownership sometimes appears without an apostrophe (attributive), Chicago omits an apostrophe only in proper names that do not officially include one; when in doubt, opt for the possessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'children’s rights; farmers’ market; women’s soccer team' but proper names like 'Publishers Weekly' or 'Diners Club' omit an apostrophe when not officially present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive with gerund
rubrics_metrics.description: A noun followed by a gerund may take the possessive form (especially with proper names and personal nouns) when the gerund is the subject; use with caution and reword if ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Fathers’ assuming the care of children has changed...' vs incorrect 'Fathers assuming the care…' when 'assuming' is participle; when the noun/pronoun follows a preposition the possessive is usually optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive with italicized or quoted terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When an italicized term appears in roman text, the apostrophe and s should be set in roman; forming the possessive of a quoted term is discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add only an apostrophe for a plural last element; avoid attempts like 'Ode on a Grecian Urn’s'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractions — apostrophe usage
rubrics_metrics.description: In contractions an apostrophe normally replaces omitted letters; use the right single quotation mark (’); colloquialisms without a clear omission (gonna, wanna) take no apostrophe; some contractions are irregular (won’t, ain’t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'singin’ (with right single quote); gov’t; ’tis (use right single quote)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractions that end in a period
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractions that end in a period (e.g., Dr.) are generally referred to as abbreviations rather than contractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interjections — spelling and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interjections (ugh, er, um, sh) appear in Webster’s; for those not listed, plausible spellings should be sought in literature or invented; the interjection 'oh' is capitalized only at sentence start, while the vocative 'O' is always capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'atchoo! shhh! Where, oh where, have you been?; “Thine arm, O Lord...”'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'a' vs 'an' before h
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'a', not 'an', before words beginning with a pronounced h; British English sometimes differs in pronouncing h; consult a dictionary when in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a hotel; a historical study' but 'an honor; an heir' where h is silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'a' vs 'an' before abbreviations, symbols, and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Before an abbreviation, symbol, or numeral, use 'a' or 'an' based on how the term is pronounced (not how it is written).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'an MS treatment (pronounced em‑ess) vs a MS (pronounced manuscript); an NBC anchor; a URL; an @ sign; an 800 number; an 007 field (oh‑oh‑seven) vs a 007‑style agent'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligature usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ligatures æ and œ in Latin or transliterated Greek words or words adopted into English; use æ for Old English contexts and œ for French contexts where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid 'Encyclopaedia Britannica' style ligatures in anglicized words; use 'œ' in French contexts like 'trompe l’oeil'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-division source and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For end‑of‑line word breaks in published (print/PDF) works, consult Webster’s as primary guide; do not apply word breaks at manuscript stage; this guidance mainly applies to print/PDF rather than reflowable electronic formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Webster’s indicates acceptable breaks between syllables; the section supplements the dictionary by offering preferred breaks and hyphenation settings for page layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word divisions to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Never divide single‑syllable words; ensure at least two letters appear before a break and at least three letters after a break; avoid divisions that carry only two letters to next line unless necessary or language‑specific exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid 'wom‑en' or 'sur‑prises' with only two letters carried; some other languages permit two‑letter carries (see chapter 11 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer word breaks that preserve pronunciation rather than derivation; choose breaks that reflect how the word is spoken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'knowl‑edge (not know‑ledge)'; 'democ‑racy or de‑mocracy (not demo‑cracy)'; be careful with words like 'project' vs 'proj‑ect'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing after a vowel
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the break affects pronunciation, words are best divided after a vowel; when a vowel forms a syllable mid‑word it should remain on the first line; treat diphthongs as single vowels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'criti‑cism (not crit‑icism)'; 'aneu‑rysm (not an‑eurysm)'; preserve vowel syllable integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing compounds, prefixes, and suffixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated or closed compounds and words with prefixes/suffixes are best divided at natural morphological breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'poverty‑/stricken (not pov‑/erty‑stricken)'; 'dis‑pleasure (rather than displea‑sure)'; 're‑inforce (not rein‑force)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing words ending in 'ing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Most gerunds and present participles may be divided before 'ing'; if the final consonant before 'ing' is doubled, break between the consonants; check dictionary for words ending in 'ling'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'certify‑ing; giv‑ing; dab‑bing; run‑ning; fiz‑zling; bris‑tling'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing proper nouns and personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: Break personal names (multi‑element proper nouns) between elements rather than within elements; if a break within a name is needed consult the dictionary; avoid breaks before numerals or Jr./Sr.; use nonbreaking spaces where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Alek‑sis; Heitor Villa‑/Lobos (or better, Heitor / Villa‑Lobos); Frederick L. / Anderson; Elizabeth II (Eliza‑/beth II if necessary)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers expressed as numerals are best left intact; if a break must occur it should come only after a comma and never after a single digit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing numerals with abbreviated units of measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeral used with an abbreviated unit of measure is best left intact; either carry the numeral to next line or move the abbreviation up; use nonbreaking spaces to prevent bad breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '345 m; 24 kg; 55 BCE; 6:35 p.m.'; spelled-out units may be broken if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division in run‑in lists
rubrics_metrics.description: A number or letter used in a run‑in list (e.g., (3) or (c)) should not be separated from the beginning of its following text; if it occurs at the end of a line, carry it to the next line or use nonbreaking space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 6.129 for run‑in list conventions; use nonbreaking space (6.121) to keep marker attached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing URLs and email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: When breaking a URL or email at line end, break between elements if possible: after a colon or double slash; before/after = or &; before a slash, period, or other punctuation; break before a hyphen rather than after it; never add a hyphen to break an address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of allowed breaks: 'http://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/' split after 'http://' or 'http://www.'; authors should not break URLs in manuscripts (2.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and line appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: For aesthetic reasons avoid more than three successive lines ending in hyphens (hyphen stack/ladder); manuscripts should not be hyphenated; in justified print text hyphenation is often necessary to avoid uneven lines; reflowable electronic formats may suppress hyphenation for aesthetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use page-layout application hyphenation settings and exceptions; limit hyphen stacks to three lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics and semantic markup for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Italics (or bold) are the default means of setting off text (emphasis, key terms, foreign words, words as words, titles); for electronic publication, use semantic markup that specifies the nature of the term to enhance accessibility (e.g., text‑to‑speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers concerned with accessibility should consult WAI/W3C and EPUB accessibility guidelines; see 2.81–83.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics for emphasis — sparing use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for emphasis only occasionally as an adjunct to efficient sentence structure; overuse reduces force; seldom italicize as much as a sentence and never a whole passage for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: unnecessary italics avoided in long phrases; italic-dependent emphasis used only when necessary (e.g., 'It was Leo!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldface or underscore for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldface or underscore may occasionally be used for emphasis (textbooks, glossaries), but in formal print italics are usually more appropriate; note any usage in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial capitals used historically for emphasis are now only appropriate ironically; capitalizing an entire word (ALL CAPS) is rarely appropriate; small caps are preferable where style needs capital emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ironic capitalization or headlines; 'POLAR ICE CAP RETURNS' is an example of all caps to avoid in formal prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicizing words from other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for isolated words and phrases from another language unless they appear in Webster’s or another standard English dictionary; if a foreign word becomes familiar through repeated use, italicize it only on first occurrence; proper nouns generally appear in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'futbol' and 'telenovelas' italicized if unfamiliar; 'pasha', 'a priori' appear in roman if in Webster’s; maintain consistency when familiar and unfamiliar terms appear together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman for familiar foreign terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words and phrases familiar to most readers and listed in Webster’s should appear in roman type and be spelled as in Webster’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'pasha; a priori; the kaiser; de novo'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman for common Latin words and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used Latin words and abbreviations (ibid., et al., ca., passim) should not be italicized; 'sic' is best italicized because of its peculiar use in quoted matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example quoted: 'mindful of what has been done here by we [sic] as agents of principle'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting key terms and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Key terms in a particular context are often italicized on first occurrence and thereafter set in roman; boldface may be used for key terms in textbooks or glossaries but such usage should be noted in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The two chief tactics—obstructionism and misinformation—require careful analysis.'; consistency between italics and boldface must be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scare quotes and their sparing use
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks used to signal nonstandard, slang, or ironic senses (scare quotes) imply distancing and should be used sparingly because they lose force and irritate readers if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Myrotary simulation app allows me to “dial” phone numbers again; avoid excessive scare quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing single and double quotation marks discouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: Using single and double quotation marks to signal different layers of meaning is sometimes done in specialized contexts but Chicago discourages this practice and prefers italics, quotation marks, and parentheses instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In philosophy one might use single for special terms and double for definitions, but alternatives are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'So‑called' does not require quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase preceded by 'so‑called' need not be enclosed in quotation marks because the expression itself signals irony or doubt; if only one part of a phrase needs highlighting, quotes may help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'So‑called child protection sometimes fails to protect' but 'so‑called “running” shoes' when emphasizing part only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common expressions and figures of speech do not need quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Common expressions, figures of speech, and slang rarely need quotation marks; reserve quotes for verbatim borrowings or ironic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Myths of paradise lost are common in folklore; I grew up in a one‑horse town.' but quoted verbatim borrowings should be in quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs, notices, and motto formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Short signs or notices are capitalized headline‑style in running text; longer notices are better treated as quotations; mottoes follow sign conventions and foreign mottoes are usually italicized with only first word capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The door was marked Authorized Personnel Only.'; 'The flag bore the motto Don’t Tread on Me.'
